figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 1. Decision tree for AI-assisted natural product development based on analytical resolution. This framework guides the selection of AI strategies 
according to the maximum achievable chemical resolution determined by available analytical infrastructure, explicitly aligning computational complexity with 
Metabolomics Standards Initiative (MSI) identiﬁcation conﬁdence levels. High-resolution workﬂows (green), supported by 1D/2D NMR (optionally integrated with MS), 
correspond to MSI level 1 and enable deﬁnitive structural conﬁrmation. In this context, structure-dependent AI platforms—including ligand-based target prediction, AI-
enhanced molecular docking, biotransformation prediction, and ADMET optimization—can be applied with high conﬁdence for pharmaceutical development. 
Intermediate-resolution workﬂows (blue), primarily based on LC–MS/MS or GC–MS data, correspond to MSI levels 2–3 and provide putative or tentative compound 
identiﬁcation. At this resolution, molecular networking and spectral similarity-based AI approaches (e.g., GNPS, SIRIUS, and CSI:FingerID) are applied in a constrained 
and supportive manner, thereby enhancing annotation conﬁdence, prioritizing structurally related features, and assisting dereplication through taxon-speciﬁc and reference
databases, rather than establishing complete structures. Low-resolution workﬂows (orange), relying on HPLC ﬁngerprints or extract-level proﬁles with minimal structural
information, preclude structure-dependent modeling. Overall, the decision tree emphasizes that AI utility in natural product research is resolution-limited rather than univer-
sally scalable and that inappropriate escalation of AI complexity beyond data resolution risks overinterpretation and reduced reproducibility. Figure created using
BioRender (https://BioRender.com). ADMET: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity; AI: artiﬁcial intelligence; GC: gas chromatography; GNPS: 
Global Natural Products Social Molecular Networking; HPLC: high-performance liquid chromatography; LC: liquid chromatography; MRD: Magnetic Resonance Data-
base; MS: mass spectrometry; MSI: Metabolomics Standards Initiative; NP: natural product; NMR: nuclear magnetic resonance; TCM: traditional Chinese medicine.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. (Main Figure). Data-quality-guided AI strategy map for natural product drug discovery. (A) Analytical infrastructure (NMR, LC–MS/MS, and HPLC/extract 
proﬁling) can be aligned with AI strategies across three MSI conﬁdence tiers, converging through an integrated WET–DRY validation l oop toward reﬁned therapeutic hypotheses
and clinical translation. (B) Decision conﬁdence matrix mapping nine AI tool categories (Table 1) against three MSI identiﬁcation tiers. Cell colors indicate the tier-appropriate role 
of each AI strategy: gray, not applicable at this tier; amber, hypothesis-supporting only (outputs should be treated as preliminary and require orthogonal experimental validation); 
blue, prioritization-strengthening (outputs can inform candidate ranking and targeted follow-up but should not be interpreted as deﬁnitive mechanistic evidence); green, 
translational conﬁdence (outputs can support structure-based inference, regulatory-facing workﬂows, and clinical translation when combined with experimental validation); 
hatched gray, future-oriented/emerging direction (NISQ-era quantum AI). Circled numerals within cells indicate suggested primary associations with orthogonal evidence 
accelerators: A1 (retrospective translational prior) contributes historically validated ethnopharmacological evidence; A2 (prospective evidence layer) contributes multi-omics-based 
mechanistic and heterogeneity resolution; A3 (structure-based reﬁnement) supports compound development via docking, MD, and structure-guided optimization. These 
represent the most direct supportive relationships rather than exclusive assignments. Translational output categories reﬂect the highest-conﬁdence application tier typically 
associated with each discovery trajectory. Two suggested benchmarks for convergent-evidence interpretation are provided: reference-matched level 1, based on authentic 
standard matching under identical instrument conditions, and high-conﬁdence level 2 criteria, based on strong spectral concordance (e.g., CSI:FingerID ≥0. 9), repeated literature
occurrence, and recurrence of known compounds. These benchmarks are illustrative and are not intended as universal thresholds. All conﬁdence assignments are qualitative and
reﬂect the current evidence landscape; they are intended as decision-support guidelines consistent with the conceptual scope of the framework. For comprehensive tool-level infor-
mation, see Supplementary Table S1 in the supplemental information online. Figure created using BioRender (https://BioRender.com). ADMET: absorption, distribution, metabolism, 
excretion, and toxicity; AI: artiﬁcial intelligence; HPLC: high-performance liquid chromatography; LC: liquid chromatography; MD: molecular dynamics; MS: mass spectrometry; MSI: 
Metabolomics Standards Initiative; NISQ: noisy intermediate-scale quantum; NMR: nuclear magnetic resonance; PBPK: physiologically based pharmacokinetic.
